title: 1492 and after
hook: Granada falls, and the Muslims of Spain are later forced to convert or leave

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alhambra, the red palace of Granada whose walls repeat one sentence. Your line was: no victor but allah.

South of Granada there's a mountain pass whose name is really a story: the sigh of the Moor. People tell that the sultan who handed Granada over, Abu Abdallah, whom the Spanish called Boabdil, rode out with his household, stopped at that pass, turned for one last look at the city and the red palace, and wept. Whether he wept there, nobody can say for certain. What came after his surrender is better documented, and it is harder to hear.
screen: `THE SIGH OF THE MOOR.` → `ONE LAST LOOK BACK.` → `WHAT CAME AFTER.`

segments.voice: Granada did not fall in a final battle. It was surrendered by treaty to Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic monarchs of Spain, and the treaty made promises: Muslims could keep their mosques, their faith, their law, their property. Those promises did not last. Before long the authorities were pressing Muslims to be baptized, and in time, across Spain, the choice became baptism or exile. Families who stayed, because home was home, were baptized, and came to be called Moriscos. Some became sincere Christians. Others kept Islam in secret, praying behind closed doors, teaching children quietly. And they wrote. Some Moriscos wrote Spanish in Arabic letters, copying prayers, stories of the prophets and rules of worship in a script their neighbors couldn't read. A language hiding inside another, so that faith could survive in a kitchen. The suspicion never lifted. There were rebellions, crushed. In the end the Moriscos as a whole, even those who were truly Christian, were expelled from Spain, crossing to North Africa and beyond. Their neighbors had been through it already. In the same year Granada surrendered, the Jews of Spain were ordered to convert or leave, and Jewish families left. Two communities, the same choice. This closes the walk through al-Andalus, and this ending belongs in the story too, beside the arches and the books. Remember the Moriscos.
screen: `SURRENDERED, WITH PROMISES.` · `BAPTISM OR EXILE.` · `SPANISH IN ARABIC LETTERS.` · `EXPELLED, AS THE JEWS HAD BEEN.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE MORISCOS.`

segments.voice: Think of a family made to leave a home they loved, the Moriscos at a harbor, or people forced from their homes today, and picture one ordinary thing they had to leave behind: a door key, a kitchen, a tree in a yard. Stay with that one thing. If you pray, remember them in whatever words are already yours; if you don't, keep them company in your attention.
Moriscos. The Muslims who stayed in Spain after Granada surrendered in fourteen ninety-two, forced to convert and, in the end, expelled. Today's word.
Your line: remember the moriscos. Faith survived in kitchens and in hidden letters. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The loss of al-Andalus and the expulsion of the Moriscos are remembered in Muslim histories, poetry and sermons; some families in North Africa trace their roots to the Moriscos.

chat.says: What happened to the Muslims of Granada after 1492?
options: Promises broke: baptism or exile, Islam kept in secret, and finally expulsion.
The treaty held, so they kept their mosques and law for centuries after.
They all left right away by choice, and no Muslims stayed in Spain.
chat.meaning: The treaty's promises didn't last. Those who stayed were baptized and called Moriscos; some kept Islam in secret; in the end all were expelled.

Boabdil.meaning: the Spanish name for Abu Abdallah, who handed Granada over

Moriscos.meaning: Muslims of Spain baptized under pressure

al-Andalus.meaning: the Muslim-ruled lands of the Iberian peninsula
